review.material: The complete primary publisher abstract was read.
review.limitations: The full 31-page paper, formal rule definitions and detailed computations were not inspected in this review.

evidence.description: Primary description of the paper’s scope and claimed contribution.

sections.title: Short overview
sections.text: Knight studies emergence in shape grammars: a computation can produce shapes not explicitly predefined, and these can then become inputs for further computation.

sections.title: Question and premise
sections.text: How can a grammar act on something its author did not anticipate? The abstract distinguishes anticipated, possible and unanticipated emergence in relation to the grammar author or user.

sections.title: Method reported
sections.text: The paper combines historical discussion with a theoretical classification and proposed special rules. It describes examples both within one grammar and across parallel grammars.

sections.title: Reported contribution
sections.text: For some problems, an action can be specified in advance even when its eventual shape target is not. The proposed rules bring certain operations previously performed outside a grammar into the grammar itself.

sections.title: What remains unchecked
sections.text: The abstract does not establish that every unanticipated shape can be handled by a predefined rule. The definitions and detailed examples need full-text review.

sections.title: Why it matters here
sections.text: Distinguish seeing a new shape from having a rule that can act on it. Keep track of which possibilities your grammar anticipates and which require new choices.

terms.meaning: In this paper’s framing, shapes not predefined in a grammar becoming available during computation.
An operation carried out outside the grammar’s specified rules.
